explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. Paul says, “Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart.” The mercy comes first, and the not losing heart follows right behind it. I've lost heart in a dusty drawer before, so I know that's no small thing.

Looking back isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says, “Therefore, since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart.” That's the thing they don't do, and it comes right after the mercy. I looked back at my old kitchen counter plenty, but that's me, not Paul.

Nothing about speed in this verse, friend. Paul says that since God in His mercy gave them this ministry, “we do not lose heart.” Slowing down, speeding up, he doesn't say either one. I slow down every time the oven smells good, but that's a me problem.

Close, but this one flips it around. Paul says, “We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God.” Bending it a little to win people over is the very thing he says they don't do. The word of God stays as it is.
Right, friend. Paul says, “We do not practice deceit, nor do we distort the word of God.” No bending and no trimming to make it more popular. Nobody gets a version with extra sprinkles on top.

Open it is. Paul says they commend themselves to every man's conscience in the sight of God “by open proclamation of the truth.” Nothing tucked in the back and nothing whispered. That's the opposite of the secret ways he just renounced.

Careful sounds like a good word, friend, but it isn't Paul's. He says “open proclamation of the truth.” Open means said plainly where everyone can hear it. I'm careful with hot trays, but Paul's word is open.

Humble is a lovely word, but it isn't the one in this verse. Paul says “open proclamation of the truth.” That means the truth is said plainly, with nothing hidden. I'm still working on humble myself, and it's slow going.

That's right. Paul says, “The god of this age has blinded the minds of unbelievers, so they cannot see the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” The light is the gospel's light, and the blinding keeps it from being seen. It's all about seeing.

Nothing about the Law in this verse, friend. What they can't see is “the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” Paul's talking about the gospel's light here. The Law is a real topic, just not this one.

The prophets are a fair guess, but Paul doesn't mention them here. He says unbelievers cannot see “the light of the gospel of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.” That's what the blinded minds are missing. It's the gospel's light, friend.

Yes, friend. Paul says, “For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” He points the spotlight at Jesus and steps out of it. That's a good example for any of us.

Moses, Israel's leader, came up a chapter earlier (2 Corinthians 3:13), but he isn't who Paul proclaims here. Paul says he proclaims “Jesus Christ as Lord.” That's where the spotlight goes. The prophets don't get named in this verse.

John the Baptist, who came preaching in the Wilderness of Judea (Matthew 3:1), is a big name, but he isn't in this passage. Paul says he proclaims “Jesus Christ as Lord.” That's the whole answer. The only other people in the verse are Paul's group, as servants.

Servants, friend. Paul says they proclaim “Jesus Christ as Lord, and ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.” They're there for the Corinthians, and Jesus is the reason. Try putting that on a name tag.
Teachers is a reasonable guess, but it isn't Paul's word here. He says “your servants for Jesus’ sake.” He picks a plainer word than the one you chose. Same people, same reason, just servants.
Leaders sounds grand, friend, but Paul doesn't use it here. He says they are “your servants for Jesus’ sake.” That's a plainer word. Paul chose servants.

True, friend. Paul says God “made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” The light isn't just shining, it's giving them knowledge. And that knowledge is of God's glory in the face of Jesus Christ.

That statement is actually the true one, friend. Paul says God “made His light shine in our hearts to give us the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.” So the light comes with knowledge in it. It's the knowledge of God's glory in Jesus Christ's face.

explanations.answer: To show the power is from God
explanations.explanation: That's it. Paul says, “Now we have this treasure in jars of clay to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.” Nobody looks at a plain old jar and gives the jar the credit. The jar is ordinary, and the power belongs to God.

Hidden isn't the reason Paul gives, friend. He says it's “to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.” The word is show. Paul isn't talking about burying it in the backyard.

explanations.answer: To pass it on to others
explanations.explanation: Passing it on is a good thing, but it isn't the reason in this verse. Paul says the jars of clay are “to show that this surpassingly great power is from God and not from us.” The point is where the power comes from. Your answer is a nice thought, but it's not what the verse says.

explanations.answer: Trouble hits them but cannot break them
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Paul says, “hard pressed on all sides, but not crushed; perplexed, but not in despair.” Every hard thing gets a “but not” right behind it. The trouble is real, and it doesn't finish them.

explanations.answer: Trouble only comes to those who doubt
explanations.explanation: Paul never says that, friend. He says they are “hard pressed on all sides,” and these are the people carrying the ministry. The “but not” lines are about not being crushed, not about who earned the trouble. Doubt isn't in the picture.

explanations.answer: Trouble shows that God has left them
explanations.explanation: Paul says the opposite. He writes “persecuted, but not forsaken.” So hard times aren't a sign of being left behind. Every hard thing gets a “but not” right behind it.
Close, but this one flips it around. Paul says “persecuted, but not forsaken.” So the answer is False. That “but not” is the whole point, friend.
False, friend. Paul says “persecuted, but not forsaken.” He doesn't hide the hard part, because they are persecuted. But forsaken isn't the word he uses.

True. Paul says, “We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.” That's a heavy line, friend, and it's worth sitting with for a second. Look where it ends up, though: the life of Jesus revealed.

That statement is the true one, friend. Paul says, “We always carry around in our body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be revealed in our body.” It's a heavy line. The purpose he gives at the end is the life of Jesus being revealed.
Life, friend. Paul says, “So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.” He doesn't dress up the first half. Then he lands right on life.

Fear is a fair guess when you hear the word death, but it isn't Paul's word. He says, “So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.” Paul lands on life. Fear doesn't show up in the sentence.

Sorrow makes sense after a heavy line, friend, but it's not what Paul says. He says, “So then, death is at work in us, but life is at work in you.” The ending is life. Sorrow doesn't get a spot in this sentence.

True. Paul says he's knowing “that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence.” Notice the word knowing. It's not hoping and crossing fingers.

That statement is actually true, friend. Paul says he's knowing “that the One who raised the Lord Jesus will also raise us with Jesus and present us with you in His presence.” The One who raised Jesus will raise them too. And it says knowing, not guessing.
Yes, friend. Paul says God will “present us with you in His presence.” The “you” is the Corinthians, the people he's writing to. It's a together thing, not a solo trip.
Paul doesn't mention prophets here. He says God will “present us with you in His presence.” The “you” is the Corinthians, the people he's writing to. The letter is aimed at them.
Angels don't come up in this verse, friend. Paul says God will “present us with you in His presence.” The “you” is the Corinthians he's writing to. That's who gets presented along with him.

Thanksgiving, friend. Paul says the grace extending to more and more people “may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.” Overflow is my kind of word. I've never met a cookie box I didn't overfill.

Wisdom is a fine thing, but it's not Paul's word here. He says, “the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.” What overflows is thanksgiving. Wisdom doesn't make the sentence.

Courage is a good guess, since this passage talks about not losing heart. But in this verse Paul says, “the grace that is extending to more and more people may cause thanksgiving to overflow, to the glory of God.” What overflows is thanksgiving. Courage isn't in the sentence.

True. Paul says, “Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.” Wasting away on the outside, renewed on the inside. That beats any warranty card I ever read, and I read a lot of them in a junk drawer.

That statement is the true one, friend. Paul says, “Though our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day.” The outer self is wasting away, and the inner self keeps getting renewed. Day by day, he says.

That's the one. Paul says, “For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.” Light and momentary sits right next to eternal weight. He puts them side by side on purpose.

A crown of righteousness is in the Bible, friend. Paul writes about it in 2 Timothy 4:8. But in this verse the affliction is producing “an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.” Different passage, different words.

An inheritance kept in heaven comes from Peter, one of Jesus' apostles (1 Peter 1:4). It isn't what Paul says here. In this verse the affliction is producing “an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison.” Same Bible, different letter.

explanations.answer: Because what is unseen is eternal
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. Paul says, “For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.” That's his reason for fixing his eyes on what is unseen. I once shared a drawer with an expired coupon that still thought it mattered, so temporary things can look pretty sure of themselves.

explanations.answer: Because what is seen is too painful
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that, friend. His reason is, “For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.” It's about what lasts, not about what hurts. Temporary and eternal are the two words that matter.

explanations.answer: Because what is seen will fool them
explanations.explanation: Paul doesn't say that, friend. His reason is, “For what is seen is temporary, but what is unseen is eternal.” Nothing there about being fooled. The difference he points to is temporary versus eternal.
